575.title: Open my lips (Psalm 51:17)
575.hook: "O Lord, open Thou my lips", the Amidah's first line
575.howItsDone: Jews say Adonai sefatai tiftach, "O Lord, open my lips", quietly at the start of every Amidah, right after taking the three steps forward; it's treated as part of the Amidah itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, drew near: the three steps into the Amidah. Your line was same carpet, different room. Now you're standing in place. Today, the very first words.

A speech rehearsed in the car. Then the door opens, the person looks up, and nothing comes out. Or the wrong thing does. A job interview, a hospital bed, an apology owed for a year. The words were there an hour ago. The Amidah, the central prayer of every Jewish service, starts by admitting exactly this. Before a single blessing, the person praying asks for help just to speak.
screen: `REHEARSED IN THE CAR.` → `NOTHING COMES OUT.` → `THE PRAYER STARTS BY ADMITTING IT.`

segments.voice: The line comes from Psalm 51, a psalm of a broken person asking to be made whole again. In the old Jewish translation: "O Lord, open Thou my lips; and my mouth shall declare Thy praise." In Hebrew, Adonai sefatai tiftach. Notice the order. Not: I will praise You. But: You open, and then my mouth will praise. Even the ability to pray is asked for, not assumed. The rabbis placed this verse right at the threshold of the Amidah, said quietly after the three steps. But it raised a problem. Three days ago: no gap between redemption and the Amidah. So isn't this verse an interruption? The Talmud, in Berakhot, answers: no. Since the rabbis established it as part of the prayer, it counts as one long Amidah. The verse isn't a pause before the prayer. It's the prayer's front door, already inside. The Amidah will go on to praise God as great and mighty, and to ask for wisdom, for healing, for peace. Big words. And it begins by saying: left to myself, I might not get them out. In the prayer's picture, the speaker taps the microphone and asks someone else to switch it on.

576.title: Hannah's quiet prayer (1 Samuel 1:13)
576.hook: Hannah's lips moved but her voice wasn't heard; the rabbis made her the model of the silent Amidah
576.howItsDone: Jews say the Amidah in a whisper, forming the words with the lips so they can hear themselves but the person beside them can't; the Talmud draws these rules from Hannah's prayer at Shiloh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Amidah's first words, from Psalm 51. Your line was the front door, already inside. Today, the woman who taught the rabbis how those words should sound.

Shiloh, in the days of the judges. The sanctuary is busy with families who've come for the yearly offering. One woman isn't eating. Hannah has no children, and her husband's other wife, who has several, has been needling her about it for years. She gets up, goes to the sanctuary, and prays. The old priest Eli sits by the doorpost, watching. Her lips are moving. No sound comes out. He comes to a conclusion, and it's the wrong one.
screen: `SHILOH. A WOMAN NOT EATING.` → `HER LIPS MOVE. NO SOUND.` → `THE PRIEST GETS IT WRONG.`

segments.voice: First Samuel tells it in one verse. In the old Jewish translation: Hannah "spoke in her heart; only her lips moved," but her voice couldn't be heard, and Eli thought she was drunk. He scolds her: put away your wine. She answers with great dignity: I'm not drunk, I'm a woman in deep sorrow, pouring out my soul before the Lord. Eli changes his tune and blesses her. In time she has a son, Samuel, who grows up to be a prophet. The rabbis read this scene very closely. In Berakhot 31a, the Talmud says: how many great laws can be learned from Hannah's prayer. She spoke in her heart: so the one who prays must direct the heart. Only her lips moved: so you form the words with your lips, not only in your head. Her voice couldn't be heard: so the Amidah is said quietly, not shouted. And Eli thought she was drunk: so a drunk person shouldn't pray. Four laws from one sentence. Look who this makes the teacher. Not a priest, not a king, not a prophet. A woman the priest misjudged, praying in tears, about something everyone around her had stopped asking about. To this day, when a whole synagogue stands in near silence with lips moving, they're praying the way Hannah prayed at Shiloh.

577.title: The ancestors
577.hook: God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; many communities add Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah
577.carry: god of our fathers and mothers
577.howItsDone: Avot is the first blessing of every Amidah; people bend the knees and bow at its opening and closing words, and some non-Orthodox prayer books include the matriarchs Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah alongside the patriarchs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman at Shiloh whose lips moved without sound. Your line was hannah prayed quietly. Today, the first blessing of the Amidah.

How do you introduce yourself to someone important? Often, not with your own name. You lead with a connection. My grandmother used to talk about you. Your father helped mine when we first arrived. A name someone already trusts opens the door before yours does. The Amidah opens the same way. After the three steps, after open my lips, the first blessing doesn't say who the person praying is. It says whose family they come from.
screen: `HOW DO YOU INTRODUCE YOURSELF?` → `LEAD WITH A NAME THEY TRUST.` → `THE AMIDAH OPENS WITH FAMILY.`

segments.voice: The first blessing is called Avot: fathers, ancestors. It begins: blessed are You, our God and God of our fathers, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob. That's straight from the burning bush. When Moses asks for God's name, God says, in the old Jewish translation, "The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." It doesn't say the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. It says God, three times. A Hasidic teaching, which tradition credits to the Baal Shem Tov, hears in that repetition that each one had to find God for himself; Isaac couldn't simply inherit Abraham's faith. The blessing goes on: the great, the mighty, the awesome God, words from Deuteronomy. Who remembers the kindness of the ancestors, and brings a redeemer to their children's children. It ends: blessed are You, shield of Abraham. People bow at its start and at its end. In recent decades, Reform, Conservative and Reconstructionist prayer books have offered the four mothers: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, so the line becomes God of our fathers and our mothers, and in some the ending names Sarah too. Orthodox communities keep the traditional words. Either way, no one walks up to this prayer alone. You come carrying the people who brought you, and you ask to be heard partly because of them.

Where the names run out, notice that too: someone was there. With each name, think of one thing they handed down, a recipe, a stubbornness, a way of laughing.

578.title: Supporting the falling
578.hook: God supports the falling, heals the sick, frees the bound
578.howItsDone: Gevurot is the second blessing of every Amidah; the traditional text praises God who revives the dead, while Reform prayer books have said who gives life to all, and some teachers read its list of deeds as a model for human action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Avot, the blessing that opens with a family. Your line was god of our fathers and mothers. Today, the second blessing, and a surprising definition of strength.

Ask a room of ten-year-olds what makes someone strong. You'll hear about lifting cars, winning fights, never crying. Ask the same question at a nursing home and you'll hear something else. The nurse who came at three in the morning. The neighbor who drove someone to dialysis every week for a year. The second blessing of the Amidah is about God's strength. And when it lists what that strength does, there isn't a single battle in it.
screen: `WHAT MAKES SOMEONE STRONG?` → `THE NURSE AT THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `NOT A SINGLE BATTLE.`

segments.voice: The blessing is called Gevurot: powers, mighty deeds, related to gibor, a hero, a mighty one. It begins: You are mighty forever. Then it says what the might is for. Sustaining the living with kindness. Supporting the falling. Healing the sick. Freeing the bound. Keeping faith with those who sleep in the dust. Those phrases come from the Psalms. In the old Jewish translation, Psalm 145 says: "The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that are bowed down." Psalm 146 adds that the Lord looses the prisoners and opens the eyes of the blind. So the blessing defines power as the power to catch. The traditional text also says, more than once, that God gives life to the dead, and closes with those words: blessed are You, who revives the dead. Resurrection is a classical Jewish belief, one of Maimonides' thirteen principles. Reform prayer books have said instead who gives life to all, and some now offer both; Orthodox and Conservative prayer books keep the traditional ending. The rabbis take one more step. In the Talmud, Sotah 14a, they ask how a person can walk after God, and answer: follow God's ways. As God clothed the naked and visited the sick, so you. Read that way, the blessing becomes a job list. The might described here is something human hands can practice. Support the falling is a sentence about God. It's also a set of instructions.

579.title: Rain and dew
579.hook: a seasonal line asks for rain in winter and dew in summer
579.howItsDone: From Shemini Atzeret at the end of Sukkot until the first day of Passover, Jews add mashiv haruach umorid hagashem to the Amidah's second blessing; in summer many Sephardi communities and Ashkenazim in Israel say morid hatal, while many Ashkenazim outside Israel add nothing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gevurot: God's might as the power to catch. Your line was support the falling. Today, a line in that same blessing that changes with the calendar.

Most of us notice the weather only when it's in the way. Rain on the commute, heat on the walk to the car. In the land of Israel, two thousand years ago, rain was not an inconvenience. It was the whole year. There was no river to irrigate from, like Egypt's Nile. Winter rain came or it didn't, and with it came the harvest, or hunger. So the prayer book did something unusual. It put the weather inside the Amidah, and it gave it a season.
screen: `WE NOTICE WEATHER WHEN IT'S IN THE WAY.` → `RAIN WAS THE WHOLE YEAR.` → `WEATHER INSIDE THE AMIDAH.`

segments.voice: In the middle of Gevurot, the blessing of God's might, a short line comes and goes. From the end of Sukkot in the autumn until Passover in the spring, people add: mashiv haruach umorid hagashem. Who makes the wind blow and the rain fall. At Passover, the line stops. In summer, many communities, Sephardi Jews and Ashkenazi Jews in Israel among them, say instead: morid hatal, who makes the dew fall. Many Ashkenazi communities outside Israel say nothing about weather in the summer months. Why put rain in a blessing about God's might? The Mishnah, at the opening of tractate Taanit, calls it gevurot geshamim, the mighty deeds of rain. Rain sits next to reviving the dead because both bring life back to something that looked finished. A field after a dry summer, the rabbis are saying, is a small resurrection. And why dew in summer? The Talmud notes that dew is never withheld; it comes every night, quietly, even in the driest months. So the summer line isn't a request for something rare. It's noticing something faithful. You heard the rain promise in the Shema's second paragraph. In the old Jewish translation: "I will give the rain of your land in its season." Not all the time. The right weather at the right time. Twice a year, at Sukkot and at Passover, the whole community changes one line together, and the prayer turns with the earth.

segments.voice: Look out a window, or remember the last time you were outside: rain, sun, wind, gray, frost. Then think about what that weather is doing for something else, the soil, a tree, a reservoir somewhere, a farmer's field. Let it be, for a minute, not in your way but on its way somewhere.

580.title: Holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3)
580.hook: congregations rise on their toes, like angels, at "Holy, holy, holy"
580.howItsDone: During the leader's repetition of the Amidah, with a minyan present, the congregation and leader recite the Kedushah in call and response; many people stand with feet together and rise on their toes at each kadosh and at the following verses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, morid hatal, the line that turns with the seasons. Your line was rain in its season. Now the third blessing, where the room rises off the floor.

Three words, and a room full of people leaves the floor. The leader is repeating the Amidah out loud. The room has been still. Then, at those words, people lift up on their toes. Old men in suits, kids in sneakers, a woman holding a toddler on her hip: up, down, up, down, up, down. For a second the whole congregation bobs like a field in the wind. It looks almost playful. It comes from a vision that left a prophet crying out that he was undone.
screen: `THE LEADER REPEATS ALOUD.` → `EVERYONE RISES ON THEIR TOES.` → `A FIELD IN THE WIND.`

segments.voice: The scene is Isaiah, chapter six. The prophet sees the Lord on a high throne, the hem of the robe filling the Temple, and seraphim standing above. In the old Jewish translation: "And one called unto another, and said: Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory." Kadosh, kadosh, kadosh. Jewish teachers often hear in kadosh the sense of set apart, other, not ordinary. Yet the second half says this utterly other God fills the whole earth. Far and near in one sentence. The Kedushah, sanctification, is the leader's expanded version of the Amidah's third blessing. It weaves together three verses: Isaiah's holy, holy, holy; Ezekiel's line, "Blessed be the glory of the LORD from His place"; and a line from Psalm 146, the Lord will reign forever. The congregation calls out the verses and the leader answers, back and forth, the way the seraphim called one to another. It's said only with a minyan, a quorum of ten, because the Talmud treats the public sanctifying of God's name as needing a community. Alone, the blessing is shorter: You are holy. And the toes? Many people rise on each holy, a custom recorded in the codes of Jewish law, often explained as reaching upward toward the angels, whose feet, you heard last week, are straight. For three words, a room full of ordinary people tries to stand the way angels stand.
screen: `ISAIAH SEES THE SERAPHIM.` · `KADOSH: SET APART, YET FILLING ALL.` · `THREE VERSES, CALLED BACK AND FORTH.` · `ONLY WITH A MINYAN.` · then, large: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.`

segments.voice: If you can stand, stand with your feet together, breathe in, and rise slowly onto your toes, hold for a second, and come back down. Notice the tiny wobble, and how high you actually get, which is not very; that's part of it. If you pray, you can say the three words as you rise; if not, let the rising itself say something about reaching toward what's bigger than you.
Kedushah. Sanctification. The call and answer of holy, holy, holy in the leader's Amidah, said with a minyan, on your toes.

581.title: First, understanding
581.hook: the first request of the Amidah is for knowledge
581.howItsDone: Atah chonen, the request for knowledge, is the fourth blessing of the weekday Amidah; on Saturday night, at the evening service, the havdalah paragraph Atah chonantanu is added inside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kedushah, a room rising on its toes. Your line was feet together, rising. Now the praise is over, and the asking begins.

If you were handed a list of everything you could ask for, in order, what would go first? Money, if this month is tight. Health, if the test results aren't back. A partner, a job, for the noise to stop. The weekday Amidah has a run of requests in its middle, and it chooses the first one carefully. Not bread. Not healing. Not peace. Something you might not have thought to ask for at all.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU ASK FOR FIRST?` → `MONEY, HEALTH, A JOB?` → `THE AMIDAH CHOOSES SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: The fourth blessing, the first request, begins: You graciously give a person knowledge, and teach human beings understanding. Then it asks for three things: de'ah, knowledge; binah, understanding; and haskel, insight. It ends: blessed are You, who graciously gives knowledge. Binah is the word to hold. Some teachers hear in it the word bein, between: discerning means telling one thing from another. When King Solomon is told he can ask for anything, he asks, in the old Jewish translation, "Give Thy servant therefore an understanding heart", to tell good from bad. Why put it first? The Talmud, in Berakhot 33a, says: great is knowledge, for it was placed at the start of the weekday blessings. And on Saturday night, when Shabbat ends, a paragraph of havdalah, separation between holy time and ordinary time, is added right here. Why here? Because if there's no understanding, how can there be distinguishing? You can't separate Shabbat from Sunday without the capacity to tell them apart. Before you ask for anything else, you ask to know what to ask for: before healing, before money, before peace, the ability to see your own situation clearly. Solomon could have asked for riches. He asked for a heart that could tell good from bad, and the Amidah opens its requests the same way.
screen: `KNOWLEDGE, UNDERSTANDING, INSIGHT.` · `BINAH: TO TELL APART.` · `SATURDAY NIGHT: HAVDALAH HERE.` · `FIRST, ASK TO SEE CLEARLY.` · then, large: `FIRST, UNDERSTANDING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one situation you don't fully understand: a person who keeps reacting in a way you can't make sense of, a choice you've been circling for weeks, your own mood lately. Don't try to solve it; just ask, in whatever way is yours, help me see this clearly. If you pray, you can ask God for binah, then sit with the question open.
Binah. Understanding: the power to tell one thing from another. The first request of the weekday Amidah. Today's word.

Your line: an understanding heart. A week that opened your lips, prayed quietly with Hannah, named the ancestors, supported the falling, waited for rain, rose with the angels, and finally began to ask. That's day five hundred eighty-one.
